## Summary

- **What Scout is:** an agent post-trained from **Inkling 2 Small** (Thinking Machines' open-weights model, launched 2026-11-05) on **Tinker**, that does research *and* prediction in a single agentic rollout. Each environment hands it a forecasting question plus tools for point-in-time research, code execution, and submitting a probability distribution. Their claim: roughly as accurate as **Fable 5.2 (medium)** at **15× lower cost per forecast**.
- **The headline chart (Figure 2):** mean log score against cost per forecast on **200 held-out numerical questions** from Metaculus, Polymarket, Kalshi and Mantic's own platform — all with prediction times **after 15 September 2026**, Inkling 2 Small's knowledge cutoff, so nothing in the eval could have been memorised from training data.
- **The 100k demo (Figure 1):** 2027 **revenue and EPS forecasts for every S&P 500 company under 50 geopolitical and economic scenarios**, each made both "as if the scenario happens" and "as if it doesn't" — one bar per forecast relative to the company's baseline (blue higher, red lower). Explicitly framed as a **scale demonstration**, not a product.
- **Three problems they had to solve to get there:**
  1. **Question scarcity.** Of ~848k numerical questions resolved on the three public platforms in 2026: ~304k remain after deduplication → ~6.6k after dropping off-topic (sports, weather, crypto prices) → **~3.9k** after dropping low-quality ones ("what someone will say, video views, next-day prices"). Fix: LLM-generated **synthetic questions from the news** (cf. Bosse et al. 2026, Turtel et al. 2026) → a pool of **45,000** quantitative questions, e.g. "How many vessels will Japan's Foreign Ministry have most recently reported as remaining in the Persian Gulf by 30 June 2026?" Validation: score gains on the synthetic questions **generalise** to the held-out public ones (Figure 4).
  2. **Research throughput.** Naively calling third-party data APIs at thousands of concurrent rollouts would have made the described run take **~9 years**. Fix: ingest those APIs continuously into their own low-latency databases — including a point-in-time copy of **Wikipedia's complete revision history (1.32 TB of indexed and embedded text)** — so the agent can semantically search "Wikipedia as it was on any past date" and batch-read historical pages in one query. The tools return only data dated before the prediction time; the resolution stays hidden.
  3. **Noisy rewards.** On any single question an over-confident forecast can outscore a calibrated one: in their simulation (Figure 6) the overconfident p₂ beats the calibrated p₁ **60% of the time**, yet p₁ is ahead by **1.16 nats on average**. Fix: a reward that mixes the outcome log score with the expected log score under a **reference forecast R** — an ensemble of frontier models run through the same harness on the same question: r = λ·log p(y) + (1−λ)·E_v~R[log p(v)] = λ·log p(y) − (1−λ)·KL(R‖p) − const. Stated trade-off: it biases toward the frontier models' errors; the outcome term keeps the reward anchored to what actually happened.
- **Training:** multi-stage post-training on Tinker at different reasoning efforts; asynchronous in-flight sampling with **StableReinforce** (3× faster experiments). Why Inkling 2 Small: its base capabilities already sit close to the forecasting Pareto frontier, it fine-tunes well, and trainer/sampler mismatch is low when served through Tinker. The harness is "deliberately lightweight and non-prescriptive" so strategies are learned rather than hardcoded.
- **What emerges through training (Figures 7–8):** at low effort the fine-tuned agent beats the base model at *lower* cost by finding the key pieces of information faster; at high effort it "works more like a quantitative analyst" — researches exhaustively and writes code to analyse data before building its final distribution (more forecasts with 20+ searches; more with 2+ sandbox code runs). Worked example — Bank of Korea's August 2026 producer price index for coal and petroleum products: **base** Inkling 2 Small made 25 tool calls and 4 code calls, read the news, fitted one straight line between the index and the oil price in won, concluded the index would fall almost as fast as oil, median **225**. **Fine-tuned:** 49 tool calls and 9 code calls; found that refinery price caps had been frozen and a fuel-tax cut ran to end-July, modelled the index month by month against Dubai crude (only ~0.38% of each 1% oil move reaches the index in the same month), stress-tested it against the 2022 oil crash (index −21% while oil −31%), median **272** expecting a slow decline.
- **Context footnote:** in the Summer 2026 Metaculus Cup, two AI systems (Mantic among them) outperformed all 600+ human forecasters for the first time.
- **Next steps (theirs):** forecasting-specific mid-training, long-horizon credit assignment, bigger datasets with curricula, scaled post-training compute.

## Why it matters

- **Direct sibling of [[2026-11-10-uncoveredalpha-frl-beat-the-street]]** — both are "AI agents forecasting company fundamentals". FRL's piece is the point-estimate-vs-consensus version (158/212 live EPS beats); Scout's 100k grid is the **conditional** version (what if scenario X happens vs not), which is the piece a plain beat-the-consensus count lacks. Neither is evidence of investment usefulness yet — both stop at accuracy or scale.
- **The transferable parts are infrastructure and reward design, not the model.** Point-in-time data plumbing (no look-ahead, resolution hidden) and a reference-regularised reward are the reusable ideas. Both map onto how to evaluate *any* forecaster honestly — the same "measure the marketed property observation by observation" standard as [[2026-11-19-sueppel-heterogeneous-ensemble-return-prediction]] and the LLM-in-finance skepticism of [[2026-11-02-quantbeckman-kg-llm-sentiment-sharpe-skepticism]].
- **Log score and calibration as the metric of record** — kin to the calibration checks in [[2026-10-21-omarsar0-decision-model-evals]]. Forecasting is judged by the probability placed on the outcome, not hit-rate; the 60%-of-the-time overconfidence simulation is the cleanest one-paragraph illustration of why in the vault.
- **Prediction markets are a thin question reservoir:** ~3.9k usable questions a year across the big three — context for the vault's prediction-market data notes ([[2026-09-01-pendulum-flow-polymarket-orderbook-archive]]). Their thesis: the universe of useful forecasts is orders of magnitude larger than what gets listed, so the training data has to be manufactured.
- **Macro/scenario angle:** 50 geopolitical and economic scenarios applied per company is the conditional-forecast shape a forecaster like [[2026-09-05-michael-ashton-e-piphany-blog]] does by hand for inflation — a template for "what does scenario X do to my exposures".
- **Skepticism gates:** (1) **self-reported** by Mantic together with Thinking Machines (the vendor of Tinker) — no third-party replication of the Pareto chart; (2) **n = 200** questions, all post-15-Sep-2026, with Mantic's own platform among the four sources — a small, partly in-house eval, no per-category breakdown in the post; (3) "15× cheaper" is **inference cost per forecast only** — training compute and the 1.32 TB data stack are not in the denominator (Models & Markets, 2026-11-25: "omitted training overhead limit the economic conclusion"); (4) "roughly as accurate" is a mean log score on one eval; (5) the 100k S&P forecasts are a **scale demo** with no outcome to score against (2027 has not happened); (6) the reference-ensemble reward inherits the frontier models' blind spots — acknowledged by the authors; (7) the demo video and the thread were not reconstructed here, the blog post was read in full.

**Isolation note (CoS convention):** personal second-brain knowledge capture only; nothing routed to the trading company.
